name: Dress
blurb: One-piece dress silhouettes from A-line to empire waist, and how dress fabric folds
title: Dress Drawing Reference: Silhouettes, Folds & Posing
description: Dress drawing reference: A-line, empire, shirt dress and other silhouettes, how dress fabric folds and moves, and how to pose and photograph a dress.
answer: A dress is a one-piece garment that covers the body and extends into a skirt. What makes one dress look different from another is mainly its silhouette, meaning where it fits closely and where it flares, plus the neckline, sleeves and length. Learning a few standard silhouettes makes dresses much easier to draw and design.

body: Think of a dress as a set of decisions: where the waist seam sits, how much the skirt flares, how long it is, and what happens at the neck and arms. Changing just the waistline changes the whole character. A high waist feels youthful or romantic, a natural waist feels classic, and no waist seam at all feels relaxed or modern.
In Japanese fandom a one-piece dress is often called wanpīsu, from one-piece, which is why some tags use that word instead of dress.

sections.h: How to draw a dress and its folds

ul: Draw the body first, then decide which points the dress touches: usually shoulders, bust and waist. Fabric hangs from those points.
Between support points the fabric falls straight down because of gravity; folds radiate from where it is pinched or gathered.
Flared skirts form tube-like folds that open toward the hem. Draw the hem as a wavy line that wraps around the legs, not a flat edge.
When one knee bends, the skirt stretches over that knee and drapes into folds on the other side.
Thin fabric clings and makes many small folds; thick fabric makes fewer, rounder ones.

body.note: A common mistake is drawing the hem as a straight horizontal line. Seen from above or below eye level, the hem is part of an ellipse.

body: Movement shows off a dress. A slow turn, a step forward or a gentle breeze lets the skirt swing and reveals the silhouette. Holding the skirt lightly at the sides, putting one hand at the waist or crossing the ankles while standing all work well.
Photographers often shoot full-length dresses from waist height so the legs are not shortened, using a 50mm to 85mm lens. Side light brings out folds and texture; flat front light hides them.

faq.q: What is the easiest dress silhouette to draw?
faq.a: The A-line, because it widens evenly from the waist and has simple, predictable folds.
An empire waist is a dress seam placed just below the bust, so the skirt falls from high on the body.

faq.q: Why do dress folds look wrong in my drawings?
faq.a: Usually the folds do not start from a support point. Mark where the fabric touches the body and let every fold begin there and fall downward.
